title: 'Silvergate' party-financing affair and resignation as Minister of Justice (2012)
description: On 22 May 2012 former Reform MP Silver Meikar wrote in Postimees that in 2009–2010 he had donated 115,000 kroons (about €7,370) to the Reform Party that was not his own money and whose origin he did not know, and that the proposal to make the donations in his name came from Michal, then the party's secretary general; according to Meikar the cash was passed on by Kalev Lillo, who then worked in the party office. Michal, by then Minister of Justice, and Lillo denied the claims and asked for an investigation; Michal said the party's financing was transparent and that he was ready to quit if the suspicions were not dispelled. The State Prosecutor's Office opened criminal proceedings the same day and later named Michal a suspect (see the justice section); it closed the case in October 2012 for lack of sufficient evidence. Meikar was expelled from the party in October 2012. The affair prompted the 'Charter 12' (Harta 12) civic petition from 14 November 2012, signed online by more than 17,500 people, and demonstrations in Tallinn, Tartu and Viljandi; President Toomas Hendrik Ilves convened a round table on party funding and civic participation. On 6 December 2012 Michal announced his resignation, saying: 'I am resigning to protect the Estonian Reform Party and the functioning of the government. It is my personal decision.' He left office on 10 December and was succeeded by Hanno Pevkur.
key_facts: Meikar's allegation published 22 May 2012; Michal and Lillo denied it
Criminal case closed in October 2012 without charges ('word against word', State Prosecutor Heili Sepp)
Charter 12 petition (more than 17,500 signatures) and protests in November 2012
Michal resigned as Minister of Justice on 6 December 2012 (left office 10 December)

title: Losses and collapse of the state airline Nordica (2023–2024)
description: As Minister of Climate, Michal exercised the state's shareholder rights in Nordic Aviation Group (Nordica). After the group reported a loss of €7.2 million on turnover of €54.9 million in the first half of 2023, its chief executive resigned and Michal ordered the supervisory board to commission a special audit of the period from 2020 to July 2023; he said the state would not provide more aid and that the company would have to be put in order for privatisation. The loss reached €11.9 million in the first nine months of 2023. The special audit, presented in early 2024, attributed the losses mainly to poor management: an expansion strategy whose risks were not assessed and a management board that did not give the supervisory board enough information. In January 2024 the government decided that Nordica would stop operating and be sold, and allocated €14.5 million to Tallinn Airport to secure routes. The privatisation failed when the prospective investor withdrew in November 2024, and the airline ceased operations and filed for bankruptcy. Prosecutors opened a breach-of-trust investigation in February 2024 and closed it in October 2025, finding no crime and naming no suspect. Michal was not a party to those proceedings.
key_facts: August 2023: Michal orders a special audit after a €7.2 million half-year loss
Special audit: losses mainly due to poor management
January 2024: government decides to wind down and sell Nordica; €14.5 million for Tallinn Airport
November 2024: investor withdraws; Nordica files for bankruptcy
October 2025: prosecutors close the investigation, no crime found

title: Tax rises, the 'security tax' and their reversal (2024–2025)
description: Postimees noted in April 2023 that there had been 'essentially no mention of possible tax increases before the elections' before Reform and its partners agreed tax rises, including a new car tax. As prime minister-designate in July 2024 Michal announced a three-part national defence tax; a Postimees editorial ('The surprise egg of the defense tax') urged him instead to cancel the planned abolition of the tax hump and cut spending. In September 2024 he promised 'tax peace' until the 2027 elections and said 'the tax festival, where every month brings a new tax proposal, will be brought to an end'. Former prime minister Mart Laar (Isamaa) wrote in November 2024 that the government had continued Kallas's approach of 'taxing the Estonian people into prosperity' and that part of the munitions to be financed by the temporary tax would only be bought after it expired. In March 2025, after removing the Social Democrats, Michal announced that the corporate profit tax and the planned taxation of personal income 'from the first euro' would be dropped; by 2026 the security tax and the planned income-tax rise to 24% had been cancelled while VAT stayed at 24%. In February 2025 Isamaa leader Urmas Reinsalu cited the government's tax rises and new taxes in an unsuccessful motion of no confidence.
key_facts: July 2024: defence tax announced (VAT, income tax, corporate profits)
September 2024: 'tax peace' until 2027 promised
March 2025: corporate profit tax and 'first-euro' income taxation dropped
2026: security tax and 24% income-tax rate cancelled; VAT 24%

title: Expulsion of the Social Democrats from the government (March 2025)
description: After months of tension, including Michal's public criticism of remarks by Regional Affairs Minister Piret Hartman (SDE) on rules for donated food, and with Reform's support at 16% in polls, Michal announced on 10 March 2025 a 'government overhaul' in which the Reform Party and Estonia 200 removed the Social Democratic Party (SDE) from the coalition. 'It is clear that there were two right-wing parties and one left-wing party in the government,' he said, adding that urgent decisions could not be debated endlessly. The change came with the cancellation of already legislated taxes and a push to end the local voting rights of non-citizens. He asked the President to dismiss the four SDE ministers on 11 March; their successors were sworn in on 25 March 2025, leaving a two-party coalition with 52 of 101 seats.
key_facts: 10 March 2025: Reform and Estonia 200 remove SDE from government
New ministers sworn in on 25 March 2025
Coalition reduced to 52 of 101 seats

title: Opposition motion of no confidence over energy and tax policy (February 2025)
description: In February 2025 opposition parties moved a motion of no confidence in Michal. Isamaa chairman Urmas Reinsalu said criticism of his energy and economic policies reflected the concerns of society, entrepreneurs and experts, and that Michal 'wants to impose subsidized energy solutions on society for an entire generation', bringing high electricity prices and supply risks; Reinsalu also criticised tax rises and new taxes and the appointment of a new state secretary. Michal replied that Estonia's long recession was ending and that growth required clean electricity cheaper than fossil fuels. The motion received 28 votes; at least 51 were needed (Babel).
key_facts: 28 MPs voted for the motion; 51 votes were needed
Opposition criticism centred on energy policy and taxes

title: Reform's exit from Tallinn's city coalition and the alleged 'Michal–Kõlvart pact' (2025)
description: In the summer of 2025 Reform left the four-party coalition governing Tallinn under Social Democratic mayor Jevgeni Ossinovski. Michal said Reform would vote for a no-confidence motion against Ossinovski and had never ruled out cooperation with the Centre Party in the capital. Reform's mayoral candidate, businessman Urmas Sõõrumaa, proposed a technocratic city government following guidelines from Reform and the Centre Party and then withdrew. Ossinovski accused Reform of a 'Michal–Kõlvart Pact' with 'secret protocols' under which Centre leader Mihhail Kõlvart would become mayor after the October 2025 elections (Via Baltica, citing ERR); this is Ossinovski's allegation. In March 2026 Isamaa MP Riina Solman wrote that Maris Lauri had first been talked into running for mayor before Sõõrumaa was chosen, and that Reform MP Pärtel-Peeter Pere had said the prime minister was behind it. In the October 2025 municipal elections Reform fell from 15 to 8 of the 79 seats on Tallinn City Council, and the Centre Party won 37.
key_facts: Reform left the Tallinn coalition and backed a no-confidence motion against Mayor Ossinovski
Mayoral candidate Urmas Sõõrumaa withdrew
Ossinovski alleged a 'Michal–Kõlvart pact'
October 2025: Reform 8 seats in Tallinn (−7), Centre 37

title: 2025 municipal election defeat and low approval ratings
description: In the municipal elections of 19 October 2025, the Reform Party's party lists won 9.97% of the national vote, behind the Centre Party (21.1%) and Isamaa (18.6%), while coalition partner Estonia 200 won 1.7%. A Postimees editorial called the result a 'red card' for the Reform Party and 'a vote of no confidence in the government'. In a Norstat poll for the Institute for Societal Research in November 2025, 28% of voters said the government was doing a good job and 18% approved of Michal's performance; in May 2026, 67% said the government was performing poorly, 21% approved of Michal, and an Emor survey found 13% trusted him. Michal remained party chairman and prime minister.
key_facts: Reform 9.97% nationally in October 2025 (Centre 21.1%, Isamaa 18.6%)
November 2025: Michal's job approval 18% (Norstat)
May 2026: government disapproval 67%, Michal's approval 21%

title: Handling of the 2026 presidential election
description: In March 2026 Isamaa MP Riina Solman accused Michal and his close circle of treating women as 'pawns', citing messages from Reform's secretary general urging the Social Democrats to put forward a female candidate as a way to sideline President Alar Karis; this is her accusation. In May 2026 Michal said Karis did not seem to have enough support in the Riigikogu for a second term and suggested former president Kersti Kaljulaid. He described Kaljulaid's removal as head of the Estonian Olympic Committee as a 'highly publicised mob attack' by 'mentally somewhat bitter and grumpy old men'; Social Democratic leader Lauri Läänemets pointed out that her opponents there included prominent Reform figures, and her foundation said no politician had approached her. Former Reform leader Andrus Ansip called Karis 'a worthy candidate'. Karis announced in June 2026 that he would not seek a second term. Michal then backed Chancellor of Justice Ülle Madise, who was elected by the Riigikogu on 2 September 2026 with 71 votes as the only candidate, after the Supreme Court rejected a challenge by nine EKRE MPs; she was due to take the oath of office on 12 October 2026.
key_facts: May 2026: Michal says Karis lacks support and suggests Kaljulaid
June 2026: Karis says he will not run again
2 September 2026: Ülle Madise elected with 71 votes; Michal had backed her

title: Failed €70 million ammunition procurement and the defence minister's resignation (2026)
description: In 2024 the Estonian Centre for Defence Investments (ECDI/RKIK) signed four contracts with Datasel, a small Italian company acquired by India's Neco Defence Munitions, and paid about €70 million in advance for artillery shells for Ukraine, funded mostly from the European Peace Facility and donor states. Usable ammunition was not delivered; the ECDI terminated the contracts in November 2025 and is pursuing the company in court and arbitration, while Datasel says it is the injured party (Estonian World). On 28 August 2026 the National Audit Office reported that, contrary to what the defence ministry had told the Riigikogu, the brokerage contracts had created risks for the state budget, with costs of about €70 million possibly falling on taxpayers, and that the Defence Forces' accounting for €1.2 billion of stocks was unreliable. Defence Minister Hanno Pevkur (Reform) resigned on 2 September 2026, taking political responsibility; before his announcement Michal said he saw no personal fault on Pevkur's part and that questions should be directed primarily at the ECDI's leaders. Coalition partner Estonia 200 had questioned whether Pevkur could stay, and the Centre Party sought support for a no-confidence vote in Michal. Michal appointed former Defence Forces commander Martin Herem, who took office on 16 September 2026 on condition that he could replace the ministry's permanent secretary and would not have to join Reform; Michal said Herem 'is not coming to be the Reform Party's Minister of Defence'. Energy and Environment Minister Andres Sutt also stepped down, saying it was his own decision. A separate criminal investigation into defence accounting failures opened in October 2025 has named no suspect; Michal is not a party to any proceedings.
key_facts: About €70 million paid in advance to Datasel in 2024; contracts terminated November 2025
National Audit Office report, 28 August 2026
Pevkur resigned on 2 September 2026; Martin Herem appointed
Michal: no personal fault by Pevkur; questions for ECDI leadership

title: Loss of the parliamentary majority and the October 2026 no-confidence vote
description: In August 2026 MP Kalev Stoicescu left Estonia 200 and MP Meelis Kiili left the Reform Party, leaving the coalition with 50 of 101 seats. Kiili said his views on national defence had diverged from the party's choices and that bills important to him had stalled without the Reform faction's support, which he had raised with the prime minister 'to no avail'. In October 2026 the opposition Isamaa, Centre Party and EKRE, joined by nine independent MPs, moved a motion of no confidence accusing the government of undermining public trust and failing to address the country's problems. It received 34 votes, short of the 51 required. The Social Democrats and several independent MPs did not sign it and abstained; their leader Lauri Läänemets said the initiators had no plan for a new government and that a government crisis would be dangerous in the security situation. Isamaa's Urmas Reinsalu said the coalition would stay in power thanks to the Social Democrats; Michal said the opposition had painted a picture of Estonia 'unrecognisable in real life' (Via Baltica, citing ERR). The Riigikogu election is due on 7 March 2027.
key_facts: August 2026: coalition down to 50 of 101 seats
October 2026: no-confidence motion gets 34 votes (51 needed)
Social Democrats abstained
